title: Same-Sex Relations in the Bible
lead: A small number of passages (Genesis 19; Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13; Romans 1:26–27; 1 Corinthians 6:9; 1 Timothy 1:10) address sex between people of the same sex. Their meaning and whether they bind today are among the most debated questions in modern Judaism and Christianity. This page sets out the main readings without taking a side.

sections.b: The texts usually discussed are Sodom's demand to "know" Lot's guests (Genesis 19:5; compare Judges 19:22), the Holiness Code's ban on a man lying with a male "in the ways of lying down with a woman" (Leviticus 18:22; 20:13), Paul's account of humans exchanging "natural relations" (Romans 1:26–27), and his words malakoi and arsenokoitai (1 Corinthians 6:9; 1 Timothy 1:10). Traditional Jewish and Christian teaching reads these as a consistent ban on same-sex intercourse, grounded in creation as "male and female" (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6). Revisionist readers argue that the texts addressed violence, exploitation, cult practice (the qadesh of Deuteronomy 23:17–18) or excess, noting that Ezekiel names Sodom's sin as pride and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50), and did not envisage faithful same-sex partnerships. Scholars such as Robert Gagnon defend the traditional reading in detail; scholars such as James Brownson defend a revised one. Jacob Milgrom and Saul Olyan offered narrower historical readings of Leviticus. See the deep section on Leviticus 18 for the arguments in full.
